name: Cullen Skink (Scottish Smoked Haddock Soup)
why: Peak winter Scottish classic — leeks, parsnip-sweet potatoes and smoked haddock in a silky cream broth. Named after the Moray Firth fishing village where haddock was smoked over driftwood, it's the ultimate mid-November soup.

steps: Trim the leeks, discard the dark green tops, and wash them well to remove any grit — chop 2 roughly and 2 finely.
Roughly chop the onions and fennel bulbs; finely chop the shallots; crush the garlic; peel and chop the potatoes into 2cm pieces.
Heat 75g butter and 1 tbsp vegetable oil in a large pan over medium heat.
Add the roughly chopped leeks, onions and fennel and gently fry for 3-4 minutes until softened.
Pour in the white wine and bring to the boil.
Add the smoked haddock and 750ml water, bring back to the boil, then reduce the heat and simmer for 30 minutes, skimming off any scum, until the haddock is cooked through.
Strain the stock and reserve it; flake the haddock into bite-sized pieces and set aside.
In the same pan, heat the remaining 75g butter and 1 tbsp oil, and fry the finely chopped leeks, shallots and garlic for 3-4 minutes until softened.
Add the potatoes and the flaked haddock.
Pour in the reserved stock, bring to the boil, reduce the heat and simmer for 10-15 minutes until the potatoes are tender.
Stir in the double cream and briefly blitz with a stick blender — just until it starts to thicken and turn creamy, keeping it rustic rather than smooth.
Ladle into warm bowls and sprinkle with chopped parsley and a pinch of freshly grated nutmeg.
Serve immediately with chunks of crusty bread.

pro_tips: Go easy on the blending — the best cullen skink has real chunks of potato, leek and fish, not a puree. A few seconds with a stick blender is enough to thicken the cream.

Use undyed (un-dyed) smoked haddock for the authentic pale colour; the red-dyed 'finnan haddie' version is fine too but will tint the soup pink. Skin on the fish while it poaches adds all the smoky flavour.
author: Henry
